_meta: A list of task durations and a worker count, used to show why uneven work should be balanced by work stealing -- idle workers pulling queued tasks from busy ones on demand -- rather than by partitioning the tasks across workers up front by count. The intuitive assignment deals tasks out round-robin, task i to worker i modulo K, so every worker gets the same number of tasks. That is only balanced if all tasks take the same time. When durations vary, equal counts are not equal work: the worker that happens to receive the long tasks has a large total and finishes late, while the workers that received only short tasks finish early and then sit idle even though the schedule as a whole is not done. The makespan -- the time until the last worker finishes -- is set by the single overloaded worker, and the idle time on the others is pure waste. Work stealing removes the up-front commitment: each worker drains its own queue, but when it empties it steals a task from the back of the most-loaded worker's queue, so work migrates from busy workers to idle ones and no worker stops while queued work remains. The makespan drops toward the ideal, the total work divided by the number of workers. This is the scheduling discipline in Cilk, Java's fork/join pool, Go's scheduler, and Rust's Rayon. On this fixture two of the eight tasks are large and, under round-robin, both fall to the same worker: static gives loads 22 and 4 (makespan 22, 18 units of idle) while work stealing gives loads 11 and 15 (makespan 15, 4 units of idle) -- a large improvement toward the ideal makespan of 13, though a coarse steal that grabs a big task late does not reach it exactly. durations is the per-task cost; workers is the number of workers. These are the fixture; the assignments, per-worker loads, makespans, and idle times are computed.
